title: Standardize token-windowing and eviction contract across continuous batching
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Problem: The continuous batching path has accumulated multiple ad-hoc windowing heuristics and eviction behaviors over time. Different components interpret a 'token window' differently (pre-split vs post-aggregation), and eviction responsibilities are split between the scheduler and the KV-backed cache. This causes three classes of issues: intermittent tail-latency spikes under mixed request shapes, duplicate token accounting leading to over-eager eviction, and opaque driver-level contention when multiple workers attempt reclamation concurrently.

Goal: Introduce a single, well-documented token-windowing contract and an eviction API boundary that cleanly separates scheduling decisions from cache lifecycle. Outcomes: reduced mutex contention in the hot path, predictable per-request token accounting for batching, and an eviction policy that is observable and tunable (priority-aware LRU with size-first heuristics).

Approach summary:
- Define a TokenWindow contract used by scheduler, batch-assembler, and KV cache. The contract specifies: inclusive/exclusive boundaries, who owns prefix/KV pointers, and how partial windows are merged.
- Extract eviction responsibilities out of the scheduler; implement a small eviction coordinator that exposes a deterministic API (ReserveWindow / ReleaseWindow / MarkHot).
- Replace the current global KV invalidation sweep with sharded, sequence-number based reclamation to avoid full-table scans.
- Remove two global locks from the continuous path: the 'hotpath_mutex' and the 'eviction_gate' by leveraging per-shard lock striping and optimistic CAS for sequence updates.
- Run a compatibility shim for two release cycles: old behavior behind a feature-flag -> opt-in -> opt-out and cleanup.

Why this approach: Centralizing the contract reduces accidental duplication, makes unit testing straightforward, and enables targeted metrics (evictions/sec, window-failures, token-accounting-mismatch-rate) to prove regressions or improvements. Sharded reclamation reduces worst-case work during eviction and avoids cross-worker stomping on the same memory regions.
acceptance_criteria: All runtime components use TokenWindow API for token accounting (scheduler, batch assembler, KV cache)
End-to-end latency P99 for mixed short+long workload improves or remains within 5% of baseline in staging
Eviction coordinator replaces in-scheduler eviction code with observable metrics (evictions/sec, reclaimed_bytes) reported to Console
No global hotpath lock in the continuous request path (verified in code review and perf shim benchmarks)
Feature flag exists to toggle new behavior; default rollout in staging, canary, then GA
tasks: Write design spec & TokenWindow API (Confluence link in attachments)
Spike: microbenchmarks comparing global lock vs sharded reclamation (2d)
Implement eviction coordinator and per-shard reclamation (engineer pair)
Refactor scheduler to call ReserveWindow/ReleaseWindow instead of inlined eviction
Add extensive unit tests for token accounting and simulated race conditions
End-to-end staging load test with mixing small chat and long-completion flows
Publish runtime telemetry and dashboards for new metrics
Rollout behind feature flag: staging -> 10% canary -> 50% -> 100%
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Incorrect accounting causes under-batching and higher costs; Mitigation: run canary with detailed token-accounting diffs and fallback to old behavior on >3% cost regression
Risk: New eviction coordinator introduces latency spikes during shard rebalancing; Mitigation: add jittered backoff and incremental shard migrations
Risk: Unexpected interaction with Dedicated autoscaler; Mitigation: coordinate with infra team and run Dedicated-specific load tests
tradeoffs: Simplicity vs runtime overhead: TokenWindow API adds an extra call boundary—we accept a small constant overhead for clearer semantics and long-term maintainability
Immediate rollout vs gradual: We'll gate on a feature flag to allow quick rollback if real traffic surfaces an edge case
migration_plan: Phase 1: Merge TokenWindow type and compatibility shim (no behavior change). Phase 2: Implement eviction coordinator behind feature-flag; run internal canary on non-critical customers. Phase 3: Expand canary, validate metrics, remove old codepaths and clean up shims in two subsequent releases.
rollout_plan: Staging -> internal canary (10% traffic) for 72h -> expand to 50% if no regressions for 48h -> full GA. During canary monitor: P50/P95/P99 latency, evictions/sec, reclaimed_bytes, token-accounting-deltas. Automated rollback if P99 increases by >10% or eviction errors >0.1%.
